title: Pee Wee Reese Puts an Arm Around Robinson
text:
In 1947 Jackie Robinson broke the color line in Major League Baseball with the Brooklyn Dodgers. He faced abuse from crowds, opposing players and even some teammates, a few of whom had circulated a petition against playing with him. Dodgers shortstop Pee Wee Reese, a Southerner from Louisville, Kentucky, refused to sign it.

According to the story told by Robinson, teammates and later writers, during a game on the road, with fans jeering and opposing players shouting slurs, Reese walked over from shortstop, stood next to Robinson and put his arm around his shoulders. He said nothing, or nothing anyone remembered. The message to the crowd was plain: this man is my teammate.

Robinson later credited Reese with helping him survive that first season. The two played together for years and remained friends. In 2005 a statue of the two men in that pose was unveiled outside the minor league ballpark in Brooklyn.
lesson: When someone is being singled out, a simple, public sign that you stand with them can change how others treat them. It costs little and may be remembered for a lifetime.
source: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (1972); Jonathan Eig, Opening Day (2007)
caveat: The date, city and even details of the gesture are disputed, and some historians doubt it happened in the form usually told.
